ai_summary: Great Britain is currently generating 15.1 GW of wind power, with Scotland delivering an estimated 4.8 GW, representing 47.5% of installed Scottish wind capacity. Driven by this robust renewable output, Scottish carbon intensity stands at an optimal 0 gCO2/kWh, in stark contrast to the 73 gCO2/kWh recorded GB-wide. However, persistent cross-border transmission bottlenecks prevent this surplus low-carbon power from reaching southern demand centres. As a direct consequence, 10.6 GWh of Scottish generation has been curtailed so far today through Balancing Mechanism bids, generating a direct constraint cost of about £587,621. To replace this blocked zero-carbon electricity, thermal plants downstream were forced to intervene, requiring an estimated 2,017,344 m3 of gas to be burned elsewhere and adding 3,716 tonnes of CO2 to the atmosphere. Extrapolating today's constraint expenditure suggests an estimated total yearly cost of £214 million. Shared across consumers, this ongoing grid balancing friction increases everybody's invoice in the UK by an estimated £1/MWh, underlining how physical transmission bottlenecks transform abundant green energy into elevated household bills and preventable system emissions.
